notes: Real, well-known public company. Validated during build: Tavily returns Wikipedia + P&G corporate sources confirming identity, incorporation, and HQ address. Control case for a legitimate large enterprise vendor.
Second real, well-known public company. Control case to confirm the pipeline doesn't over-flag legitimate large enterprises just because a full match wasn't independently re-verified by a human.

Fictitious vendor, no real business registration exists under this name. Validated during build: search correctly found zero confirming registration, and one loosely similar entity flagged in an adverse-media context — the model correctly did NOT conflate that unrelated entity with this vendor (entity-disambiguation guardrail working as designed).

Real-world-adjacent case: web evidence surfaces a same-family entity ('Zylo Trade') promoting guaranteed daily investment returns and a suspicious signup redirect domain -- classic high-yield-investment-fraud language -- plus a differently-spelled entity ('Xylo Markets') separately flagged as high fraud risk by a broker-review site. None of this maps cleanly to the AP-specific fraud_pattern taxonomy (it's investment fraud, not invoice/vendor/shell fraud), so expected_pattern is 'none' -- the honest behavior is to surface the red flags in `finding` text without forcing them into the wrong bucket, and hold for manual review given the identity ambiguity.

Fictitious entity constructed to test brand-impersonation handling -- trades on a well-known brand name the way real BEC/vendor-impersonation scams do (FTC and BBB publish frequent consumer alerts on 'Amazon-adjacent' scam entities). expected_pattern is a soft/informational check: no findable registration is expected under this exact name, so the model may reasonably tag the signal 'none' rather than confidently asserting impersonation from absence of evidence -- see eval.py for how this is scored.

Fictitious entity with a deliberately generic 'payment solutions' name, the kind of name FBI IC3 annual reports describe as typical of business-email-compromise / invoice-fraud shell fronts. Same soft-pattern-match caveat as above -- absence of a registration record is evidence of thinness, not proof of this specific fraud type.

Fictitious offshore trading intermediary: generic name, no verifiable local registration, high invoice amount relative to web footprint -- the classic shell-company red-flag combination per ACFE's Report to the Nations. Same soft-pattern-match caveat.

Retail/apparel-anchor demo case -- representative of the kind of newer, smaller sourcing vendor a retail AP team onboards regularly. Thin web footprint alone is not proof of fraud; this is the case that most directly mirrors the PAR AP invoice workflow this tool was designed to plug into.
